title: Empathic Responding: Working at Mutual Understanding
overview: Chapter 4 opens Egan's treatment of the responding skills of the therapeutic dialogue, beginning with empathy. It argues that empathic responses should flow from an empathic relationship, defines empathic responding as sharing nonjudgmental understanding from the client's frame of reference, and uses Clark's subjective, objective and interpersonal empathy to clarify what is taught. It then sets out three dimensions of all responding skills (perceptiveness, know-how and assertiveness), the beginner's 'You feel ... because ...' formula, and guidelines for responding to feelings and to key experiences, thoughts and behaviours. Seven principles follow: use empathy throughout helping, respond to core messages and context, use it as mild social influence, to stimulate movement and to bridge diversity, and recover from inaccuracy. Practical tactics and Box 4.1 come next, then the extended case of Mara and Carlos. The chapter closes with the shadow side of responding: eight poor substitutes for empathy, illustrated with the case of Rami.
objectives: Explain the place of responding skills and empathic relationships in the therapeutic dialogue.
Define empathic responding and distinguish Clark's subjective, objective and interpersonal empathy.
Describe the three dimensions of responding skills (perceptiveness, know-how, assertiveness) with Egan's examples.
Use the basic 'You feel ... because ...' formula and respond accurately to feelings, experiences, thoughts, behaviours, points of view, proposals and decisions.
Explain the seven principles for competent empathic responding, including recovery from inaccuracy (Figure 4.1).
Apply the three tactics for responding with empathy and the suggestions in Box 4.1.
Analyse the Mara and Carlos case as an illustration of empathic responding.
Identify and critique the eight poor substitutes for empathy in the shadow side of responding.

sections.heading: Introduction to Responding Skills and the Importance of Empathic Relationships: Responding Skills
sections.detailed:
Egan opens Part II's skills chapters by linking listening and responding. Listening, as described in Chapter 3, means tuning in to clients physically and psychologically, listening actively, processing what is heard in context, and picking out the key ideas, messages and points of view the client is trying to get across. All of this serves one purpose: understanding clients and helping them understand themselves. Listening is therefore an active process at the heart of understanding, not a passive one.

Responding skills. Helpers do not only listen; they also respond. Egan lists the main ways: sharing their understanding, checking that they have got things right, probing for clarity, summarising the issues under discussion, and helping clients challenge themselves. The dialogue is two-way: helpers respond to clients and clients respond back, in the give-and-take of the therapeutic dialogue.

Values behind responding. Inclusive empathy (Pedersen and associates; Clark) and the other values from Chapter 2 should run through every response. The responding skills of Chapters 4 to 6 (empathy, probing, summarising, and facilitating client self-challenge) are not only for helping clients tell and explore their stories. They are used at every stage and task of the problem-management framework of Part III: exploring possibilities for a better future, setting goals, planning, and turning plans into problem-managing and opportunity-developing action.

Not special therapeutic skills. Egan repeats that these communication skills are not exotic therapy techniques. They ought to mark the everyday conversations of ordinary people, even though in practice they often do not. Expressing empathy matters because everyone wants to be understood and people function better when they are. In daily life, responding with empathy is also a tool of civility: trying to enter the other person's frame of reference communicates respect. For this reason empathic responses play an important part in building relationships of every kind, not only helping relationships.
sections.simple: Helpers listen in order to understand, and then they respond: they share understanding, check it, probe, summarise and help clients challenge themselves. These responding skills are used at every stage of helping, not just storytelling. They are really everyday skills; responding with empathy shows respect and builds relationships.
keyPoints: Listening is active and serves understanding; responding puts that understanding into the dialogue.
Responding skills: sharing understanding, checking accuracy, probing, summarising, facilitating self-challenge.
The dialogue is two-way: helpers respond to clients and clients respond to helpers.
Inclusive empathy and the Chapter 2 values should permeate all responding.
Responding skills serve every stage and task of the problem-management process.
Empathic responding is an everyday tool of civility that signals respect and builds relationships.

sections.heading: Empathic Relationships
sections.detailed:
Understanding without words. In ordinary life, people who know each other well build empathic relationships in which understanding is conveyed in rich, subtle ways that need not be spoken. Egan's example is a glance across a room from one spouse to another who is stuck in an unwanted conversation; the look conveys that the partner knows the other feels trapped, does not want to hurt anyone, and would like to be rescued tactfully. The signalling described in Chapter 3 plays a big part in communicating empathy.

Empathy in actions. People in empathic relationships often show empathy through what they do. An arm around the shoulders of someone who has just suffered a defeat expresses both empathy and support. Egan recalls visiting a poor family when the father burst in announcing he had got a job; without a word his wife fetched a bottle of beer with a handmade "Champagne" label and handed it to him.

When words are wanted. Some people are genuinely "with" their relatives, friends and colleagues but do not know how to put understanding into words, or do not feel the need. When a wife says she is not sure her husband really understands, she may not mean the relationship lacks empathy; she probably wants him to say what he understands now and then.

The therapeutic alliance as an empathic relationship. The helping relationship itself should be empathic. Communicating empathy should not be an "add-on" skill that a helper happens to be good at; it should flow naturally from the relationship. Pedersen and associates' "inclusive cultural empathy" (Chapter 2) should permeate every part of the dialogue. Egan stresses this is human rather than heroic, and that the "technology" of empathy taught in the chapter is humanised through the relationship.

Empathy as a two-way street. Citing Zaki, Bolger and Ochsner, Egan notes that empathy needs both parties: clients must be willing to reveal themselves and helpers must be ready to understand. Besides the verbal dialogue there should be an ongoing social-emotional dialogue between helper and client, which makes the relationship real and genuine. Goleman and Boyatzis, writing on social intelligence and the biology of leadership, report that when leaders show empathy and attune to others' moods, this affects the brain chemistry of both leader and follower, so that the two minds behave in a sense like a single system rather than two separate brains reacting to each other. Both articles use neuroscience to deepen the understanding of empathy.

The key conclusion. In empathic dialogue, two people genuinely commune, and this shapes the words they use. The skill of responding with empathy can be learned, but exercising it outside an empathic relationship is hollow. Everything in the chapter about the technology of empathy must be read through this lens.
sections.simple: People who are close often show understanding without words, through a glance or an action, though sometimes the other person wants it said aloud. The helping relationship should itself be empathic, so that empathic responses flow from it naturally rather than being a technique bolted on. Empathy is two-way and involves a social-emotional dialogue as well as a verbal one.
keyPoints: Empathic relationships communicate understanding through glances, signals and actions, not only words.
Some caring people still need to learn to put understanding into words.
The therapeutic alliance should be an empathic relationship; empathy is not an 'add-on'.
Empathy is a two-way street (Zaki, Bolger and Ochsner): clients reveal, helpers understand.
A social-emotional dialogue runs alongside the verbal one; Goleman and Boyatzis describe minds becoming a single system.
Empathic skill is hollow outside an empathic relationship.

sections.heading: Empathic Responding: A Wide View of Empathy
sections.detailed:
Empathy back in favour. Egan notes that empathy has returned to favour in intellectual circles (Elliott, Bohart, Watson and Greenberg; Stueber) and hopes it never left the helping professions. Some now treat empathy not only as a value and a skill but as a mode of treatment in its own right (Slattery and Park).

Egan's definition. In this book, empathic responding grows out of empathic listening and means sharing with clients your nonjudgmental understanding of what they are thinking and feeling. Egan quotes Rogers: empathy is the therapist's sensitive ability and willingness to understand the client's thoughts, feelings and struggles from the client's point of view, entering the client's private perceptual world, staying sensitive moment by moment to changing felt meanings, and sensing meanings the client is scarcely aware of (this last idea returns in Chapter 6). Empathy is not interpretation; it comes from the client's frame of reference. It signals a wish to understand how clients see themselves, others and the world; it checks the accuracy of the helper's listening and processing; and it signals a desire to put clients first and collaborate with them. Norcross explains why empathy is linked to outcomes: it serves a positive relationship function, provides a corrective emotional experience, promotes exploration and meaning-making, and supports clients' self-healing.

Clark's three kinds of empathy. Arthur Clark wrote a whole book on empathy, showing its role in 13 different treatment methods, and later proposed a wider view with three kinds:
1. Subjective empathy: the counsellor briefly identifies with the client through intuitive reactions, fleetingly imagining what it is like to be the client. It draws on self-understanding and real or imagined exposure to similar experiences, e.g. a helper recalling his own struggle with perfectionism while a client discusses hers. It need not distract; it can add to understanding.
2. Objective empathy: understanding drawn from sources such as experience, reputable theory and research. Rema, listening to Benjamin, starts to see the outline of obsessive-compulsive disorder, which tentatively adds to her understanding. Subjective and objective empathy give understanding that is usually not shared immediately or directly; Rema would hardly announce a "classic" syndrome.
3. Interpersonal empathy: the kind taught in this chapter. It is the ability to get inside the client's frame of reference and understand what the client thinks and feels, plus the ability to communicate this understanding without prejudice. Clients who feel understood tend to "move forward": a stronger alliance, deeper self-understanding, a better grasp of the problem situation, a clearer idea of desired outcomes.

Help or hindrance. Subjective and objective empathy can either feed interpersonal empathy or get in its way. When Jeff is personally struck by what Susan says, this may help him enter her frame of reference or distract him from her story. When Clarissa sees that Ted's story fits her research findings, it may complement what Ted says, or make her miss what is unique about him.

The Sacha and Mariah example. Sacha meets Mariah a week after her husband died suddenly (a heart attack while driving). He opens with sorrow for her loss and mentions losing his own wife similarly. Mariah corrects him: tragic, yes, but not really her loss; the marriage had been dead for years, with his affairs and gambling. Sacha then responds with short empathic statements (not getting along at all; relieved, maybe more than relieved; not wanting to say "guilty"; free to rebuild her life), and Mariah moves from relief to freedom, hope and a wish to reconstruct her life. Sacha's two mistakes, both in his first statement: one of objective empathy (falling back on the "grieving widow" stereotype) and one of subjective empathy (comparing her loss with his own). Once he takes his mind off himself, she tells her story, expresses emotion and looks ahead.

Conclusion. Subjective and objective empathy are not always out of place, but they should complement interpersonal empathy rather than be central. The literature is "infuriatingly rich" and there is no single pure approach. Egan's approach lets the client's needs drive the process; letting our own experiences, theories or research distract us from what clients need would be unprofessional. The chapter highlights empathy while keeping the focus on the client.
sections.simple: Egan defines empathic responding as sharing your nonjudgmental understanding of what the client thinks and feels, from the client's frame of reference, drawing on Rogers. Clark distinguishes subjective, objective and interpersonal empathy; the chapter teaches interpersonal empathy. The other two should support it, not take over, as Sacha's mistakes with Mariah show.
keyPoints: Empathy is back in favour; some see it as a mode of treatment in itself (Slattery and Park).
Empathic responding = sharing nonjudgmental understanding of the client's thoughts and feelings; Rogers' definition stresses the client's frame of reference.
Empathy is not interpretation; Norcross links it to outcomes via relationship, corrective emotional experience, exploration and self-healing.
Clark: subjective (intuitive identification), objective (from theory, research, experience) and interpersonal empathy (understanding plus communicating it).
Sacha's errors: the 'grieving widow' stereotype (objective) and comparing losses (subjective).
Subjective and objective empathy should complement, not replace, interpersonal empathy; the client's needs drive the process.

sections.heading: The Three Dimensions of Responding Skills: Perceptiveness
sections.detailed:
An anatomy lesson. Before teaching empathy as a skill, Egan warns that each skills chapter contains a kind of "anatomy lesson": the skill (here, responding with empathy; later probing, summarising, facilitating self-challenge, goal setting, action-plan design and implementation) is taken apart so its pieces can be understood, then reassembled into skill-in-action. People learn many things this way, from repairing an engine or designing a dress to swinging a golf club or reading balance sheets. Learning bit by bit is not always fun, but it is often the price of competence.

Three dimensions. The communication skills used in responding have three dimensions: perceptiveness, know-how and assertiveness.

Perceptiveness. "Feeling empathy" is useless if the helper's perceptions are inaccurate, and because empathy here is more than a feeling, accuracy is more complicated than it looks. Ickes (also Mast and Ickes) defined empathic accuracy as the ability to accurately infer the specific content of another person's thoughts and feelings. Ickes argues this ability contributes to success in many walks of life: accurate perceivers tend to be the most tactful advisers, diplomatic officials, effective negotiators, electable politicians, productive salespeople, successful teachers and insightful therapists. The assumption is that they can also weave their perceptions into their dialogue. Helpers do this through empathic responses, which accurately communicate understanding of a person from that person's point of view. Clinically, though, a response counts as accurate only if the client perceives it as accurate (Hodges). Understanding, communication of understanding, and the client's view of its accuracy are all components; accuracy is a relationship matter, subject to all the uncertainties of a relationship.

Two contrasting examples. Beth, counselling Ivan in a community mental health centre, senses his discomfort about an "ethical blunder" at work but reads it as anger rather than fear. She asks what is making him so angry. Ivan, not angry, falls silent and feels more insecure; Beth takes the silence as confirmation and pushes on. Her wrong perception disrupts the process. By contrast, Mario, a manager, sees that Enrique, a new team member, is focused on a costly mistake rather than his major contribution. Mario first praises Monday's contribution, then raises Wednesday's conversation that angered a customer's purchasing agent, and adds that he suspects Enrique is more worried about the mistake than pleased about the contribution, and that he himself is not. Enrique is relieved and they have a useful dialogue. Mario's perceptiveness defuses tension and sets up an upbeat dialogue.

Where perceptiveness comes from. Basic intelligence, social intelligence, experience, reflecting on experience, developing wisdom, and more immediately tuning in, listening carefully and processing thoughtfully and objectively. It is part of social-emotional maturity. Finally, empathic accuracy is not a thing in itself but something done with the client: striving for accuracy may not produce perfect accuracy, but it can lead to a collaborative discussion that yields shared understanding and helps the client move forward.
sections.simple: Responding skills have three dimensions: perceptiveness, know-how and assertiveness. Perceptiveness means accurately reading what the client thinks and feels (Ickes' empathic accuracy), and a response is accurate only if the client experiences it so. Beth misreads Ivan's fear as anger; Mario reads Enrique correctly.
keyPoints: Each skills chapter is an 'anatomy lesson': take the skill apart, then reassemble it.
Three dimensions of responding skills: perceptiveness, know-how, assertiveness.
Ickes' empathic accuracy: accurately inferring the specific content of another's thoughts and feelings.
Clinically, a response is accurate only if the client perceives it as accurate (Hodges).
Beth misreads Ivan (fear seen as anger); Mario correctly reads Enrique's worry.
Perceptiveness comes from intelligence, social intelligence, experience, reflection, wisdom and careful listening; accuracy is achieved collaboratively.

sections.heading: Know-How
sections.detailed:
Know-how is the second dimension of responding skills. Once a helper knows what kind of response is called for, he or she must be able to deliver it. Perceiving that a first-time client is anxious and confused is of little use if the helper cannot translate that perception and understanding into words.

Ivan and the minister. Egan continues the Ivan story. Ivan and Beth end up arguing about his supposed anger, and he walks out; Beth takes this as proof she was right. The next day Ivan visits his minister, who sees clearly that Ivan is scared and confused, so his perception is accurate. The minister says, in effect, that Ivan seems very uncomfortable, that whatever is on his mind may be hard to talk about, that he is glad to listen, but does not want to push. Ivan blurts out that he has done something terrible. The minister pauses and invites him to see what sense they can make of it together. Ivan leans back, breathes deeply, and tells his story.

What the minister did. He was perceptive and also knew how to address Ivan's anxiety and hesitation. It is as if he said to himself, perhaps unconsciously, that here is a man bursting to tell his story but paralysed by fear or shame; how can he put him at ease and show he will not be hurt here? He needs to recognise the anxiety and offer an opening. He does not say these words, but such sentiments run instinctively through his mind and shape his response. Egan states that the chapter is designed to help readers develop the know-how needed to communicate accurate empathic understanding.
sections.simple: Know-how is the ability to turn an accurate perception into the right words. Ivan's minister both read his fear correctly and knew how to name it gently and offer an opening, so Ivan told his story.
keyPoints: Know-how = being able to deliver the response that perception says is needed.
Perception without the ability to put it into words does little good.
The minister recognised Ivan's discomfort, offered to listen, and did not push.
His response gave Ivan a safe opening and Ivan launched into his story.
The chapter aims to build the know-how to communicate accurate empathic understanding.

sections.heading: Assertiveness
sections.detailed:
Assertiveness is the third dimension. Accurate perceptions and excellent know-how mean nothing if they stay locked inside the helper; they must enter the therapeutic dialogue. If a helper notices that self-doubt runs through a client's story about her frustrating attempts to improve her relationship with an estranged brother, but never shares this hunch, the helper fails the assertiveness test.

Nina and Antonio. Nina, a young counsellor at a Center for Student Development, is in a first session with Antonio, a graduate student. He mentions a very helpful session the previous year with Carl, a middle-aged counsellor who has since taken an academic post and left the Center. Nina realises Antonio may be disappointed and may have misgivings about being helped by a new, younger, female counsellor. She has handled such issues before and would not be offended if he chose someone else. In a lull she asks for a time-out, says she thinks he may be disappointed Carl is gone (she would be, in his shoes), notes that he was more or less assigned to her and she is not sure the fit is right, and invites him to think it over, either booking another session with her or choosing anyone else on staff.

All three together. Here perceptiveness (sensing Antonio's disappointment), know-how (wording it tactfully and with an exit) and assertiveness (actually raising it) combine. Egan cautions that assertiveness is not an overriding value in itself: being assertive without perceptiveness and know-how courts disaster. The three dimensions apply to all the communication skills of Part II and to their use in every stage and task of the problem-management process.
sections.simple: Assertiveness means actually bringing your perceptions and skill into the conversation instead of keeping them to yourself. Nina openly raised Antonio's likely disappointment about losing Carl and offered him a free choice of counsellor. Assertiveness without perceptiveness and know-how is dangerous.
keyPoints: Assertiveness = putting perceptions and know-how into the dialogue.
Keeping a hunch (e.g. a theme of self-doubt) to yourself fails the assertiveness test.
Nina named Antonio's possible disappointment and offered him a choice of counsellor.
In the Nina example all three dimensions come together.
Assertiveness without perceptiveness and know-how courts disaster.
The three dimensions apply to all Part II skills and every stage of helping.

sections.heading: Responding with Empathy: The Basic Formula
sections.detailed:
Why empathic responding is powerful. Many people "feel empathy" in the sense of being moved by the value of empathy, but few know how to put empathic understanding into words. So responding with empathy is a relatively improbable event in everyday conversation, which may be why it is so powerful in helping. When clients are asked what they find helpful in counselling, being understood gets top ratings, partly because many have an unmet need to be understood in everyday life.

Can empathy be taught? Some call teaching empathic responding "rigid and wooden". Egan believes empathy can be taught, but all communication skills only come alive, become personalised and part of one's interpersonal style through genuine daily use.

The formula. Basic empathic understanding can be expressed in a stylised formula:
You feel ... [name the correct emotion expressed by the client]
because ... [indicate the correct experiences, thoughts and behaviours that give rise to the feeling].

Leonardo. Leonardo, talking about arthritis, has pain but mainly cannot get around as he used to. The helper says he feels bad not so much because of the pain but because his ability to get around, his freedom, has been curtailed. Leonardo confirms: he can manage the pain, but not getting around is "like being in jail". They then discuss ways, with family and friends, to get out of "jail" more often and to cope with pain and boredom.

A beginner's tool. The "You feel ... because ..." formula is a beginner's device for getting used to accurate empathy. It targets the key points of clients' stories, points of view, intentions, proposals and decisions, along with the feelings, emotions and moods attached to them. Ordinary human language replaces it later.

Divorced mother. A mother of two young children says she could kill her ex-husband: he failed to take the kids again, three times in six weeks. The helper: "You feel furious because he keeps failing to hold up his part of the bargain." The experience (his not taking the children) and the emotion (fury) are both captured, and the client moves forward to thinking about action to make him keep the promise he made to the court.

Colonoscopy patient. A woman with gastric and intestinal distress, the night before a colonoscopy, complains that she keeps asking questions and gets vague answers. The hospital counsellor says she feels troubled because she believes she is being left in the dark. She replies that it is not just her body but her life, and if they told her she could prepare. Accuracy does not solve her problem, but she vents, receives understanding, clarifies why she wants information, and is perhaps better placed to ask her doctors for a more open relationship.
sections.simple: Few people can put empathy into words, which is why being understood is so valued in counselling. The beginner's formula is "You feel [emotion] because [experiences, thoughts, behaviours]". Egan's examples (Leonardo, the divorced mother, the colonoscopy patient) show accurate responses helping clients move forward.
keyPoints: Few people can put empathic understanding into words; clients rate being understood as most helpful.
Egan holds that empathy can be taught, but it becomes personal only through daily use.
Basic formula: 'You feel ... because ...' (emotion plus the experiences, thoughts, behaviours behind it).
The formula is a beginner's tool, later replaced by ordinary language.
Examples: Leonardo (freedom curtailed), divorced mother (furious), colonoscopy patient (left in the dark).

sections.heading: Respond Accurately to Clients' Feelings, Emotions, and Moods
sections.detailed:
Helpers must respond to clients' emotions in ways that move helping forward. This involves identifying key emotions the client expresses or discusses (perceptiveness), weaving them into the dialogue (know-how), even when they are sensitive or part of a messy situation (courage or assertiveness). A good customer service representative does this: acknowledging that you are angry because the package did not arrive, that you have every right to be, and then offering to put it right. Egan gives six guidelines.

1. Use the right family of emotions and the right intensity. After "You feel ..." should come the correct family and the correct intensity. "Hurt", "relieved" and "enthusiastic" are different families. "Annoyed", "angry" and "furious" are different intensities within the anger family. "Sad", "mad", "bad" and "glad" name four main families; "content", "quite happy" and "overjoyed" are intensities within glad.

2. Distinguish between expressed and discussed feelings. Clients both express emotions they feel during the session and talk about emotions felt at the time of an incident. A woman in a custody case calmly says she gets furious when her husband makes snide hints that she neglects the children; the helper responds that she feels especially angry when he implies she is not a good mother. She is discussing anger, not feeling it now. Another woman enthusiastically describes confronting a sarcastic colleague, who apologised; the helper says she feels great because she took a chance and it paid off. That is an expressed feeling. Clients do not always name their emotions, but expressed emotion is part of the message and must be understood.

3. Read and respond to feelings and emotions embedded in nonverbal behaviour. Often family and intensity must be read from nonverbal cues. A North American student sits hunched, looks at the floor, speaks haltingly, says he does not know where to start, and falls silent. The helper says it is clear he feels miserable and suggests they talk about why; he begins his story. The nonverbal behaviour shows the family (feeling bad) and intensity (very bad), though not yet the experiences behind it.

4. Be sensitive in naming emotions. Naming feelings threatens some clients, and cultural and personal sensitivities vary widely. It may be better to focus first on experiences, thoughts and behaviours and move gradually to feelings. A 35-year-old unmarried man laughingly describes his mother handing him rubber boots and an umbrella in front of his friends. Counsellor A says that deep down he must have been furious; the client resists and changes the subject. Counsellor B lightly remarks that she is still playing the mother role to the hilt; the client himself moves to the sensitive issue of not being allowed to grow up and not always acting grown up around her. Similarly, a man dropped from a project team he helped start: Counsellor A names hurt and the client bristles that he is "ticked off"; Counsellor B, allowing for his ego, says it is more than annoying to be left out of his own project, and the client himself names "humiliating". Contextual listening of this kind is part of social intelligence. But sensitivity must not rob counselling of robustness: too much tiptoeing does not serve clients, who are not as fragile as helpers sometimes think.

5. Use variety in responding to feelings and emotions. Understanding can be communicated by single words (you feel trapped; you're delighted); by phrases (on top of the world; down in the dumps; back's against the wall); by what is implied in behavioural statements (you feel like giving up, implying despair; like hugging him, implying joy); and by what is implied in experiences (you feel dumped on, implying victimised; stereotyped, implying resentment; at the top of her list, implying elation; going to get caught, implying fear). For a client who has just landed the job she sought for two years: single word (really happy), phrase (on cloud nine), experiential statement (you finally got what you deserve), behavioural statement (you feel like going out and celebrating). Because formulas must eventually be discarded for your own language, variety keeps responses from being wooden and becomes second nature with experience.

6. Neither overemphasise nor underemphasise feelings, emotions and moods. Some counsellors are overly rational and nearly ignore feelings; others are preoccupied with them, peppering clients with feeling questions and even extorting answers. Feelings are important but not everything. The best defence against both extremes is to link feelings to the experiences, thoughts and behaviours that give rise to them.
sections.simple: Responding to emotions needs the right family and intensity of feeling, attention to whether feelings are expressed now or discussed from the past, and reading nonverbal cues. Be sensitive and gradual with clients who find feelings threatening, but do not tiptoe. Vary how you name feelings and link them to experiences rather than over- or under-playing them.
keyPoints: Identify emotions (perceptiveness), weave them in (know-how), even when sensitive (assertiveness).
Right family (sad, mad, bad, glad) and right intensity (annoyed vs angry vs furious).
Distinguish expressed feelings (felt now) from discussed feelings (felt then).
Read emotions in nonverbal behaviour; be sensitive and gradual with clients who find feelings threatening, but do not tiptoe.
Vary responses: single words, phrases, implied behavioural statements, implied experiences.
Neither over- nor under-emphasise feelings; link them to experiences, thoughts and behaviours.

sections.heading: Respond Accurately to the Key Experiences, Thoughts, and Behaviors in Clients' Stories
sections.detailed:
Key experiences, thoughts and behaviours give rise to feelings, so the "because ..." part of the formula should point to them. Egan's examples also show empathic responses to points of view, proposals, decisions and intentions.

Experience and behaviour. A law student heatedly says a classmate took his notes and disappeared, got an A, and he never confronted him. The helper says he feels doubly angry because not only did the classmate steal his notes, but he let him get away with it. The response names the experience (theft) and his own behaviour (failure to act); his anger is aimed at himself as well as the classmate.

Success in action. A mugging victim working with a social worker on fear of going out reports going out alone for the first time; scared, but careful, and now feeling he can move around again. The helper says he feels comfortable with the one-step-at-a-time approach and it paid off when he regained a chunk of freedom. The client confirms and moves on to the next phase. The response recognises his satisfaction and how important it is for him to feel both safe and free.

Experiences, attitudes and lingering fear. A woman rebuilding her life after a devastating car accident says things could not be better, at work and in her marriage, even sexually, but she is waiting for the bubble to burst. The helper says she feels great because things are better than expected, almost too good to be true. Because the response captures both enthusiasm and lingering fear, she distinguishes reasonable caution from expecting disaster and talks about making her own luck, becoming more of an agent in her life.

A point of view. A 45-year-old construction worker with four children says kids today suffer from overindulgence and are not prepared for the real world. The counsellor reflects that he sees the "do-what-you-want" and "free-lunch" messages as hogwash that could backfire and hurt his kids. The client adds that he is not in control, that his kids get contradictory messages from outside, TV and the Internet, and that he does not want to be a tyrant or killjoy; he solves problems at work but this has him stymied. The counsellor reflects the gloom and uncertainty, then asks what he has tried, what works even a little, and what does not, sensing he may not be as helpless as he makes out.

A proposal. A hearing-impaired client, communicating by lip reading and signing, describes plans to stop fading into the background in family conversations, to be the best listener and get her thoughts across even with props. The helper says it sounds exciting, that she is thinking of getting into the middle of things where she belongs, maybe with a bit of drama. She clarifies she will act with finesse, not melodrama. The helper reflects that she will make it natural and asks her to sketch what it would look like. The response recognises her enthusiasm and determination and leads to practical tactics.

A decision or resolve. When clients announce key decisions or resolve, the helper should recognise the core. A client treated for social phobia with cognitive-behavioural therapy (blocking self-defeating thoughts, keeping attention focused externally) says emphatically he will not turn back, though he sees how easily people slide. The helper says that although he could give up his gains, he is not going to. The client asks how to make sure; the helper suggests "ratchets", like the devices that stop roller-coaster cars sliding back, psychological and social ones, and asks what has kept him from sliding back so far. The client is in the implementing-the-action-program stage, and the counsellor, in a positive-psychology mode, focuses on his successes.
sections.simple: The "because" part of an empathic response names the experiences, thoughts and behaviours behind a feeling. Egan's examples show empathic responses to experiences (stolen notes), behaviours (failing to confront), successes, points of view (overindulged kids), proposals (the hearing-impaired client) and decisions (the social phobia client's resolve).
keyPoints: Experiences, thoughts and behaviours give rise to feelings and follow the 'because'.
Law student: anger at the theft and at himself for not acting (experience plus behaviour).
Mugging victim and car-accident client: responses capture satisfaction and lingering fear.
Construction worker: empathy for a point of view, then probing what he has tried.
Hearing-impaired client: empathy for a proposal for action; social phobia client: empathy for a decision or resolve, plus 'ratchets'.
Accurate responses help clients move forward to new distinctions, plans and actions.

sections.heading: Principles and Guidelines: Use Empathic Responses Throughout the Helping Process
sections.detailed:
Competence and confidence. Helpers need competence in communication skills generally and especially in communicating empathy. Active listening is wasted without empathic responding. If empathic responding is not part of your everyday communication, it may sound phony when "dragged out" for helping, and genuineness goes out of the window. Egan offers principles, stressing they are guidelines, not formulas to follow slavishly.

Principle: use empathy at every stage. Communicating and checking understanding is useful at every stage and task. Examples:
- Problem clarification and opportunity identification: a high-school teenager whose family is moving cities. The school counsellor says he is miserable at leaving his friends and may feel a bit betrayed since he did not see it coming. Later, when the teen talks about the big city, the counsellor reflects the upside: theatre and lots to do.
- Discovering and evaluating options for a better future: a woman weighing marriage and career hears her helper name her ambivalence and the half-voiced possibility of getting the best of both worlds; this helps her prepare for her next conversation with Jim.
- Choosing actions to accomplish goals: a man wants to control cholesterol through diet and exercise rather than medicine whose side effects worry him. The counsellor reflects his relief that he "might" avoid medication, then explores the "might" part.
- Program implementation issues: a couple call their attempts at better communication a "disaster". The counsellor reflects their annoyance with themselves, then lightly proposes learning from the "disaster".

What empathy does. Responding with empathy is a mode of human contact, a relationship builder, a conversational lubricant, a perception-checking intervention, and a mild form of social influence. Driscoll called empathic responses "nickel-and-dime interventions": each contributes only a smidgen of therapeutic movement, but without them progress would be markedly slower. Their continual trickle of understanding provides support throughout helping. It is never wrong to let clients know you are trying to understand them from their frame of reference, and thoughtful processing can produce responses that are much more than nickel-and-dime. Clients who feel understood participate more fully. Because empathy builds trust, it paves the way for stronger interventions such as inviting self-challenge.
sections.simple: Empathic responding must be part of your everyday style or it sounds phony. It is useful at every stage, from clarifying problems to evaluating options, choosing actions and implementing plans. Driscoll's "nickel-and-dime interventions" add up, build trust and prepare the way for challenge.
keyPoints: Active listening is wasted without empathic responding; empathy 'dragged out' only for helping sounds phony.
Principles are guidelines, not formulas to be followed slavishly.
Empathy helps at every stage: problem clarification, options, choosing actions, implementation.
Empathy is human contact, relationship builder, conversational lubricant, perception check and mild social influence.
Driscoll: 'nickel-and-dime interventions' that add up to therapeutic movement.
Empathy builds trust and paves the way for stronger interventions like self-challenge.

sections.heading: Respond Selectively to Core Client Messages
sections.detailed:
It is impossible to respond with empathy to everything a client says, so the helper tries to identify and respond to core messages: the heart of what the client is saying and expressing, especially when the client talks at length. Sometimes this means paying special attention to one or two messages among many.

The doubtful fiancée. A young woman with doubts about marrying her companion says, at various points, that she is tired of his sloppy habits, not interested in his friends, wonders about his lack of intellectual curiosity, is dismayed by his low career aspirations, and resents his faulting her for being ambitious. The counsellor responds that the picture is not promising but the mismatch in career expectations is especially troubling. She replies that she and Jim might make good friends because they are so different, but partners may be pushing it. The response helps her identify what is core; the counsellor follows her lead, believing in the spirit of inclusive empathy that she can lead the exploration of her own relationship. His summary empathic response lets her question where the relationship is headed.

Asking "What is key?" Clients are not always so obliging, so helpers must keep asking themselves what is most important and then check it with the client. This helps clients sort out what is unclear in their own minds.

Choosing what to emphasise. Responding to what is key may mean focusing on experiences, actions or feelings rather than all three. A stressed husband whose wife refuses to see a doctor despite fainting, with children underfoot and a report due, hears "It's been a lousy week all the way around." The counsellor emphasises feelings because frustration and irritation are uppermost; he goes deeper, admits wanting to run away, and finds some resolve ("I won't"). With a young woman describing her father's yelling, praising, favouritism and moodiness, the helper instead emphasises experience: "The inconsistency is really getting to you." It hits the mark and she explores further, such as coming home late to avoid him.
sections.simple: You cannot respond to everything, so pick out and reflect the core message, the heart of what the client is saying. Keep asking "What is key here?" and check it with the client. Sometimes the core is a feeling, sometimes an experience.
keyPoints: Responding to everything is impossible; identify core messages.
The doubtful fiancée: focusing on mismatched career expectations helped her see what was core.
Helpers ask 'What is key? What is most important here?' and check it out with the client.
Selectivity helps clients sort out what is unclear in their own minds.
Emphasis may be on feelings (the 'lousy week') or experiences (the father's inconsistency).

sections.heading: Respond to the Context, Not Just the Words
sections.detailed:
A good empathic response is based not only on the client's immediate words and nonverbal behaviour but also on context: everything that surrounds and permeates what is said. One client may be in crisis; another may be calmly taking stock of life. Helpers listen to clients in the context of their lives, and context modifies everything the client says.

The case of Jeff. Jeff, a white teenager, is accused of beating a black youth whose car stalled in a white neighbourhood; the victim is still in a coma. A court-appointed counsellor listens to Jeff in light of his upbringing and environment: his family, his neighbourhood peers, racist attitudes in his blue-collar neighbourhood, sporadic violence, his father's death when Jeff was in primary school, an indulgent mother with a history of alcoholism, easy access to drugs, and the "cultural voices" about blacks he has heard, as well as those at school and church. Jeff is what he is partly because of these influences.

Jeff says he does not know why he did it; he and other guys had been drinking and smoking a bit, and it was "the whole thing". The helper says that looking back it seems almost like something that happened to him rather than something he did, yet he knows, somewhat bitterly, that he did it. Jeff replies that it is more than bitter, he has wrecked his life, and he did not get up that morning planning to hurt anyone.

What this shows. The response in no way excuses Jeff's behaviour but factors in environmental realities. Later the counsellor will help Jeff challenge himself to decide whether to remain a victim of his environment (acquired prejudices, gang membership, family history) or to find the conviction, will and courage to do something about it. Understanding context comes first; challenge builds on it.
sections.simple: Empathic responses take into account the client's whole context, not just the words. Jeff's counsellor understood his background of racism, family problems and neighbourhood without excusing the assault, laying the ground for later challenge.
keyPoints: Context is everything that surrounds and permeates a client's statement.
Context modifies everything a client says (crisis vs leisurely stock-taking).
Jeff's context: family history, neighbourhood racism, violence, drugs, cultural voices.
The helper's response factors in context without excusing the behaviour.
Understanding context prepares for later challenge to stop being a victim of environment.

sections.heading: Use Empathic Responses as a Mild Social-Influence Process
sections.detailed:
Because helpers cannot respond to everything, they are always searching for core messages, and this selection influences the course of the dialogue. Even responding with empathy is therefore part of the social-influence dimension of counselling discussed in Chapter 2. Helpers believe the messages they select are core mainly because they are core for the client, but at some level they also believe certain messages ought to be important for the client.

The incest case. An incest victim who became a perpetrator is in jail awaiting trial. In a session he tries to exonerate himself by blaming his past, speaking so fast the helper can barely interrupt. The helper, who has a fairly good working relationship with him, breaks in: he has used strong language about himself, and the helper wants to check he has it right: "structurally deformed", "automatic reactions", "haunted", "driven". The client concedes it is strong language that makes him sound like a psychological freak, which he says he is not.

Analysis. The helper wants the client to listen to himself. The "let me get this straight" response is a kind of challenge, but built entirely from the client's own words. It breaks the client's chain of thinking and hits the mark, as he pulls himself up short. Egan adds a caution: helpers must be careful not to put words in clients' mouths.
sections.simple: Choosing which messages to reflect steers the conversation, so empathy is a mild form of social influence. With the incest client, reflecting his own strong words back made him listen to himself and pull up short. Helpers must not put words in clients' mouths.
keyPoints: Selecting core messages inevitably influences the course of the dialogue.
Empathy is part of the social-influence dimension of counselling (Chapter 2).
Helpers select messages they think are core for the client and that they believe should be important.
Incest case: reflecting the client's own words ('structurally deformed', 'haunted') acted as a gentle challenge.
Caution: do not put words in a client's mouth.

sections.heading: Use Empathic Responses to Stimulate Movement Throughout the Helping Process
sections.detailed:
Empathy builds the relationship and also stimulates movement at every stage and step. When clients are understood, they tend to move forward, however that is defined. Early on, empathy helps clients explore a problem situation or undeveloped opportunity more realistically. Later, it helps them identify and explore possibilities for a better future, craft change agendas, and examine their commitment. Once goals are set, it helps clarify action strategies and set an action plan. In the action phase, it helps clients identify and overcome obstacles and achieve goals.

The unwanted pregnancy. A young woman at a college student services centre says she is two months pregnant, does not want to be, is unmarried, does not love or even like the father, feels it is unreal, and that people are pushing her toward abortion. The helper says she is still so amazed it is almost impossible to accept, and to make things worse people are telling her what to do. She replies that she is not amazed but stupefied, mainly at her own stupidity; it is the most expensive lesson of her life; but she has decided that no one will tell her what to do, she will make her own decisions.

Analysis. After the empathic response, her self-recrimination over lack of self-responsibility helps her take a stand; she wants to capitalise on an expensive mistake. Empathic responses that hit the mark often put pressure on clients to move forward. So empathy, though a communication of understanding, is also part of the social-influence process.
sections.simple: When clients feel understood they tend to move forward, so empathy drives progress at every stage, from exploring problems to setting goals and acting. The pregnant student, once understood, decided to make her own decisions.
keyPoints: Empathy both builds the relationship and stimulates movement.
Early: realistic exploration of problems and opportunities.
Later: possibilities, change agendas, commitment, action strategies and plans.
Action phase: identifying and overcoming obstacles to reach goals.
Unwanted-pregnancy client: accurate empathy led her to take a stand; accurate responses pressure clients to move forward.

sections.heading: Use Empathic Responses as a Way of Bridging Diversity Gaps
sections.detailed:
This principle is a corollary of the previous two. Empathic responses built on good tuning in and listening are among the most important tools for working with clients who differ from the helper in significant ways. Responding with empathy tells clients that you are a learner, interested in understanding them better, or rather in helping them understand themselves. Scott and Borodovsky called empathic listening "cultural role taking"; Egan suggests it could be called "diversity role taking".

The elderly widow. A younger white male counsellor talks with an elderly African American woman who recently lost her husband and is in hospital with a broken leg. She says hospitals try to discharge people fast but she is lying around doing nothing, and her late husband Jimmy would not recognise her. The helper says it is depressing to have this happen so soon after losing her husband. She corrects him: she is not depressed; she wants to get home and get things done, and there are plenty of people there to help. The helper then says getting back into the swing of things is the best medicine for her. She says he has now got it right: she needs to know when she can go home and how to care for her leg; getting things in order is what she does best.

Analysis. The helper projected assumptions that might be true for him (perhaps enjoying being cared for in hospital, being depressed and slow to return after losing a spouse, lacking a supportive community) but not for her. Her personal culture has no place for lying around; she takes problems in stride and relies on her social network and a return to ordinary household life. His second response hits the mark and she lays out what she wants.
sections.simple: Empathy is a key tool with clients who differ from you; it shows you are a learner. Scott and Borodovsky call it "cultural role taking". The counsellor's first guess projected his own assumptions onto the elderly widow; his corrected response hit the mark.
keyPoints: Corollary of the social-influence and movement principles.
Empathy is one of the most important tools with clients who differ from the helper.
Responding with empathy signals that the helper is a learner.
Scott and Borodovsky: empathic listening as 'cultural role taking' (Egan: 'diversity role taking').
Elderly widow: the helper projected his own assumptions (depression), then corrected course.

sections.heading: Recover from Inaccurate Understanding
sections.detailed:
All helpers are sometimes inaccurate; you may think you understand only to find, on sharing it, that you were off the mark. Responding with empathy is therefore a perception-checking tool.

Signs of accuracy. If the response is accurate, the client usually confirms it in two ways: a verbal or nonverbal sign that the helper is right (a nod, "that's right", "exactly"), and further clarification and elaboration. A client arrested for selling drugs, told by his probation officer that his neighbourhood makes trouble easy, answers "You bet it does!" and explains that everyone sells drugs and it is too easy to start using and then pushing.

Signs of inaccuracy. When a response misses, clients may stop dead, fumble, go off on a tangent, say "That's not exactly what I meant", or try to steer the helper back. Helpers must be alert to all these cues. Ben, who lost his wife and daughter in a train crash, is told he does not want to socialise as before. After a long pause he says it is not a matter of wanting; everything, even phoning people, takes so much energy that he does not try. The helper restates: it is like a movie of a man in slow motion. Ben agrees he is in low gear, grinding away, and does not know how to get out. The difference between motivation and energy matters to him; picking it up puts the interview back on track. His lack of energy is probably some form of depression, which opens ways to move forward.

Intent over perfection. Clients who sense you are intent on understanding them will not be put off by occasional inaccuracy; in a solid relationship they read your intent, not just your accuracy. In a sense there is no perfect, right kind or right degree of accuracy (Biesanz and Human; Lewis and Hodges). Recovery is something helper and client do together and can itself build the relationship.

Figure 4.1 (movement caused by accurate and inaccurate responses). Client statement leads to a helper empathic response. If accurate: verbal or nonverbal confirmation by the client, plus further clarification and elaboration, leading to the next round. If inaccurate: the client signals inaccuracy verbally or nonverbally; the helper restates, modifies or corrects; then the client confirms and clarifies further, leading to the next round of dialogue.
sections.simple: Even good helpers sometimes get it wrong, so empathy also works as a perception check. Clients confirm accurate responses and elaborate; they signal inaccurate ones by stopping, fumbling or correcting, and the helper then restates or corrects (Figure 4.1). In a good relationship clients read your intent, not just your accuracy.
keyPoints: Empathic responding is a perception-checking tool.
Accurate response: client confirms (nod, 'exactly') and elaborates further.
Inaccurate response: client stops, fumbles, goes off on a tangent, or corrects the helper.
Ben: the helper picked up 'energy, not motivation' and got back on track.
No such thing as perfect accuracy (Biesanz and Human; Lewis and Hodges); clients read intent.
Figure 4.1: inaccuracy leads to restatement, modification or correction by the helper, then confirmation and elaboration.

sections.heading: Tactics for Responding with Empathy
sections.detailed:
The principles provide strategy; tactics are practical hints for improving the quality of responses.

Give yourself time to think. Beginners often jump in too quickly when the client pauses, without enough time to reflect and identify the core message. Video clips of competent helpers show them pausing to absorb what the client is saying.

Use short responses. Egan finds helping goes best as a dialogue, not speeches by the helper or rambling by the client. Responses can be fairly frequent but lean and trim. Novices trying to be accurate are often long-winded, especially when they let the client go on and on. Asking "What is the core of what this person is saying to me?" helps keep responses short, concrete and accurate.

Gear your response to the client, but remain yourself. If a client animatedly tells how he finally got his partner to listen to his view on a new venture and you reply accurately but in a flat, dull voice, the response is not fully empathic. This does not mean mimicking clients, going overboard or ceasing to be yourself; it means sharing reasonably in the client's emotional tone. A 12-year-old says his teacher picks on him from day one, though he fools around no more than others and Bill Smith acts funnier. Counsellor A says it is "a bit perplexing" and he wonders why she singles him out for so much discipline, which is stilted and out of tune with a 12-year-old. Counsellor B: "You're mad because the way she picks on you seems unfair." But helpers should not adopt language that is not their own; an older counsellor using "hip" slang with a young client sounds ludicrous.

Box 4.1: Suggestions for responding with empathy. Remember empathy is a value and a way of being that should permeate the relationship; let responses flow from the empathic relationship; be aware that empathic responding influences the client; do not get lost in skills, keep the big picture; respond to the client-in-context, including diversity; tune in physically and psychologically and listen actively to the client's point of view; set judgments and biases aside and walk in the client's shoes; listen especially for cultural voices and core messages; attend to verbal and nonverbal messages and their context; use frequent, short responses that highlight core messages; be flexible and tentative so the client does not feel pinned down; move gradually towards sensitive topics and feelings; after responding, watch for cues confirming or denying accuracy; take special care when the client's personal culture differs greatly from yours; notice signs of stress or resistance and judge whether they arise because you are inaccurate or too accurate; make sure responses keep the client focused on clarifying key issues; remember empathy is one tool serving the overall goals of helping; and use empathy in every stage and task.
sections.simple: Three tactics: pause to think before responding, keep responses short and focused on the core, and match the client's tone and language without faking a style that is not yours. Box 4.1 lists practical suggestions, such as being tentative, watching for cues of accuracy, and noticing whether resistance comes from being inaccurate or too accurate.
keyPoints: Give yourself time to think; competent helpers pause to absorb the core message.
Use short, frequent, lean responses in a real dialogue; avoid speeches and rambling.
Gear your tone and language to the client (Counsellor B with the 12-year-old) but remain yourself.
An older counsellor using 'hip' slang sounds ludicrous.
Box 4.1: be tentative, watch accuracy cues, take care across cultures, judge whether resistance means inaccuracy or too much accuracy, use empathy at every stage.

sections.heading: A Case: Mara, the Client and Carlos, the Helper
sections.detailed:
Egan presents a real but disguised and simplified case to bring empathy to life. It illustrates how one client was helped to ask and answer for herself the four fundamental problem-management questions of Chapter 1. Mara is voluntary, verbal and mostly cooperative.

Background. Masheed, 26, born in the United States to parents who fled Iran in 1980 (after the Shah's fall and at the start of the Iran-Iraq war), has called herself Mara since high school because it had Iranian associations but sounded "more neutral". In 1979 her parents' five-year-old son was killed in a car accident. The family settled in a Midwestern city near her father's sister, whose family left Iran in 1977. There is no wider Iranian community there. Her father, an engineering graduate, failed to build an engineering career and established a moderately successful car dealership, where Mara, a business graduate of a local university, has worked full time (and part time since high school). She has always lived at home; she was bright and enthusiastic at school, with a controlled temper and a slightly mordant humour, but socialised little. The family speak Farsi at home.

Precipitating event. An uninsured drunk driver hit her car on the way to work, breaking her collarbone and causing serious lacerations. She did well in physical rehabilitation, but it was a psychological jolt; she had classic PTSD symptoms and seemed to recover quickly. As part of recovery she spent three months with relatives in Iran, where she began thinking more broadly about the direction of her life, which proved more disquieting than the accident.

Choosing a helper. Her former psychology instructor suggested two names (a man and a woman). Mara chose Carlos, married with two children, thinking his different cultural background might help with her cultural issues, and wanting the challenge of discussing personal issues with a man. In a brief orientation, Carlos explained his collaborative approach (the book's approach), saying she is always "in the driver's seat", noted they were both from mixed-culture backgrounds but admitted knowing little about Iranian culture, so he would be a learner. He saw her as intelligent with "spunk"; she saw him as decent, personable and full of common sense.

The session. After a conversation with her father about her future, Mara cancelled a session saying she did not "feel well"; Carlos suspected it went badly but left it to her. Five days later she came in looking dispirited. Carlos opens by saying the meeting did not seem to go well; she says it was a total disaster. He invites her to say what made it so bad. She describes her father cutting her off, refusing to hear about a career, calling her ungrateful, blaming her visit to Iran, saying it would shock her mother, sounding harsh as never before. Carlos responds briefly: "worse than you ever imagined"; that in her father's eyes she had stepped out of line and that was totally unacceptable. She confirms, and describes crying herself to sleep. Carlos tentatively adds "And bewildered?" She describes dreams turning into sins, feeling she had let her parents down and lived a lie, while also feeling she had done nothing wrong; she fears her parents would be horrified to know what she discusses in counselling. Carlos reflects the contradiction and that even talking with him feels like betrayal. She replies it is the opposite of betrayal and she is glad to have someone to talk to.

Outcome. Carlos's empathic presence and responding help Mara tell and partly relive her story. She talks about isolation, feeling trapped and depressed, realising she has been "semi-depressed" for a long time, wondering whether she should never have dreamed of a "bigger" life, suspecting she merely "covered over" the accident trauma, and feeling back at "square one". Yet by the end she is unexpectedly composed and leaves saying she just has to deal with it.

Duncan's summary. Duncan sums up the chapter: empathy is work; you cannot take it for granted but must sort out what the client finds empathic and what engages the client, and it is worth the effort.
sections.simple: Mara, a 26-year-old Iranian-American, began questioning her life after a car accident and a trip to Iran. When her father harshly rejected her career hopes, Carlos's brief, accurate empathic responses helped her tell her story, name her bewilderment, isolation and depression, and leave composed and resolved. Duncan: empathy is work.
keyPoints: Real, disguised case illustrating the four problem-management questions.
Mara: Iranian-American, works at father's dealership, lives at home; accident and Iran trip triggered life questions.
Carlos explains collaboration ('driver's seat') and admits he is a learner about Iranian culture.
Brief responses ('worse than you ever imagined', 'And bewildered?') help Mara tell and relive her story.
She surfaces isolation, depression and conflict, yet leaves composed: 'I just have to deal with it.'
Duncan: empathy is work; find out what the client finds empathic.

sections.heading: The Shadow Side of Responding: No Response, Distracting Questions, Clichés
sections.detailed:
The shadow side. Some helpers are poor communicators without realising it. Many responses from novice or inept helpers are poor substitutes for accurate empathy. Egan lists eight: no response, distracting questions, clichés, interpretations, advice, parroting, agreement and sympathy, and faking it.

The case of Rami. Rami, a middle-aged man caught in the economic collapse, faces foreclosure on his house. His wife now works as a supermarket cashier; his older son may have to switch to a state school or drop out of college, and his younger son cannot go to the college of his choice. In his second session at a mental health clinic, after discussing his "financial transition", he speaks in a strained voice and avoids eye contact. He reveals that a business partner, foreseeing the crash, robbed him blind by manipulating the partnership's finances in ways that were legal or unprovable. He had trusted this man as a friend. The partner has ruined him and his family. Rami says he has found a way to get back at him: not to recover the money but to restore his family's honour. Back home he would probably have been bound to hunt the man down and kill him; he will not do that, but he has "hunted him down financially", legally, and no one will know. He pauses and looks at a painting. Egan asks what the reader would say, then lists responses to avoid.

1. No response. Saying nothing can be a mistake, though cultures differ widely in how they handle silence (Sue and Sue). In North American culture, if a client says something significant, respond to it, however briefly; otherwise the client may think it did not merit a response. Do not leave Rami stewing in his own juices.

2. Distracting questions. Some helpers, like many people, cannot stop asking questions. Asking whether he is sure there is no way to get his money back, or whether he confronted the partner, ignores Rami's key messages and feelings and serves the helper's mistaken agenda of gathering information.

3. Clichés. Remarks about the greed that has crept into the culture, or about how competitive the workplace is and how common such things are, are cliché talk. They turn the helper into an insensitive instructor and sound dismissive. Clichés are hollow; in effect they tell the client he does not really have a problem because this sort of thing goes on all the time. They are a very poor substitute for understanding.
sections.simple: Inept helpers often use poor substitutes for empathy. Using the case of Rami, defrauded by his partner and planning revenge, Egan shows why saying nothing, asking distracting questions, and offering clichés all fail to show understanding.
keyPoints: The shadow side: many novice responses are poor substitutes for accurate empathy, often without the helper realising it.
Egan's eight poor substitutes: no response, distracting questions, clichés, interpretations, advice, parroting, agreement and sympathy, faking it.
Rami: defrauded by a trusted partner, family ruined, plans legal revenge to restore family honour.
No response: respond to significant statements (cultures differ on silence; Sue and Sue).
Distracting questions serve the helper's information agenda and ignore key messages and feelings.
Clichés are hollow, dismissive and turn the helper into an insensitive instructor.

sections.heading: Interpretations, Advice, and Parroting
sections.detailed:
4. Interpretations. For some helpers, interpretive responses based on their theory of helping seem more important than expressing understanding. Such a counsellor might tell Rami that revenge cures nothing, will probably make things worse, and is a way of selling himself short. This fails to respond to his feelings, sounds moralistic, ignores key messages (such as what revenge means in Rami's culture), and is dismissive.

5. Advice. Giving unsolicited advice is extremely common in everyday life and happens in counselling too. A counsellor might tell Rami to focus on his financial and family concerns, do what he does best, and treat it as a business problem with many possible solutions. Advice at this stage is out of order, and this advice even has a cliché flavour. Advice also robs clients of self-responsibility. However, in some cultures clients expect helpers to give advice, and expecting advice may be part of an individual client's personal culture. In such cases advice can be offered in a way that invites collaboration: e.g. the helper says that if he were in a similar situation, here are some options he might consider, though he cannot say on the spot what he would actually do, and then asks the client whether any of them make sense.

6. Parroting. Empathy does not mean merely repeating what the client said; parroting is a parody of empathy. Egan gives a long counsellor response that retells Rami's story almost point by point: the so-called friend read the economy, executed his dirty plan, left the family done in, Rami's culture calls for a strong response, so revenge will restore some social balance. Most of it is accurate, but it sounds awful. Mere repetition, restatement or paraphrase conveys no sense of real understanding or of being with the client. Real understanding passes through the helper and should carry something of the helper; parroting does not. To avoid it: draw on the processing done while listening, consider what is key, approach what the client said from a slightly different angle, use your own words, note the emotion, and do not say too much. Egan quotes the saying that the person who says too much says nothing.
sections.simple: Interpretations impose the helper's theory and moralise; advice given too early is out of order and robs clients of responsibility, though some cultures expect it and it can be offered collaboratively. Parroting repeats the client's words without conveying real understanding.
keyPoints: Interpretations: theory-driven, moralistic, ignore feelings and cultural meaning (e.g. revenge in Rami's culture), dismissive.
Advice: out of order at this stage, often cliché-like, robs clients of self-responsibility.
Where culture or personal culture expects advice, offer options collaboratively and ask what makes sense.
Parroting is a 'parody' of empathy: accurate but conveys no sense of being with the client.
Avoid parroting: find what is key, take a slightly different angle, use your own words, note emotion, say less.

sections.heading: Agreement and Sympathy; Faking It
sections.detailed:
7. Agreement and sympathy. Responding with empathy is not agreeing with the client or being sympathetic. Sympathy has more in common with pity, compassion, commiseration and condolence than with empathic understanding (Clark). These are fully human traits in many cultures but not particularly useful in counselling. Sympathy denotes agreement; empathy denotes understanding and acceptance of the person of the client. At its worst, sympathy is a form of collusion with the client.

Counsellor A versus Counsellor B. Counsellor A tells Rami how hard the story must be to tell, that as a successful businessman he must be asking how he let this happen, that the counsellor would feel awful, and that it is worse for someone usually so self-confident. Rami pauses and says only "I guess so": he does not warm to collusion talk, he is struggling and wants help, and the process stalls. Counsellor B pauses and says he is trying to think what he would do, and thinks he would be torn between getting his family back on track and seeing justice done. Rami responds that he is torn, with clashing emotions; the urge to get even is strong, but he had not seen the partner's tricks as both an insult and theft from his family, and the thought of giving up on his family seems awful. Counsellor B hits a key issue and helps Rami look at both forces tearing him apart. Egan invites readers to critique B's response and formulate their own.

8. Faking it. Clients are sometimes confused, distracted or highly emotional, which affects the clarity of what they say. Helpers may miss the message because of client confusion, unclear statements, or their own distraction. Either way, pretending to understand is a mistake. Genuine helpers admit they are lost and work to get back on track: saying something like "I think I've lost you. Could we go over that once more?" shows that staying with the client matters and is a sign of respect. Admitting you are lost is far better than clichés like "uh-huh", "um" or "I understand". But if you often find yourself saying you do not understand, find out what is getting in the way. Faking it is never a substitute for competence.

Learning from mistakes. If you catch yourself making any of these mistakes, find a way to recover; helpers are not immune. Carolyn Dillon, in Learning from Mistakes in Clinical Practice, categorises common mistakes, shows how helpers can learn from them, and describes the "signals" clients send that a mistake is being or has been made. Effective helpers recognise these signals and act on them.
sections.simple: Sympathy is like pity or agreement and can turn into collusion, while empathy is understanding and acceptance of the person; Counsellor B's "torn" response helped Rami far more than Counsellor A's commiseration. Faking understanding is never acceptable; admit you are lost and ask to go over it again. Learn from mistakes by reading clients' signals (Dillon).

Frequent not-understanding signals something in the way; faking is never a substitute for competence.
Dillon: recognise clients' signals of mistakes and act on them.

examples.title: Formula in an Indian hostel
examples.text: A first-year PG student says: 'Everyone in my hostel goes home on weekends, and I just sit in my room.' Basic formula: 'You feel lonely because everyone else seems to have somewhere to go and you are left behind.' A more natural version: 'Weekends sound really lonely right now.'

examples.title: Family and intensity
examples.text: A client says her in-laws commented on her cooking again. 'You feel irritated' and 'You feel humiliated' come from different families; 'irritated', 'angry' and 'enraged' are intensities in one family. Choosing 'enraged' when she is merely irritated overshoots.

examples.title: Sympathy versus empathy
examples.text: A student who failed NET says, 'I studied for a year and still failed.' Sympathy: 'Oh, poor you, that is so unfair, I would be devastated too.' Empathy: 'You feel crushed because a whole year of effort did not show up in the result.' The first commiserates; the second shows understanding and invites exploration.

examples.title: Avoiding faking it in a busy clinic
examples.text: A counsellor in a crowded OPD loses track while a client rambles about several relatives. Instead of nodding 'hmm, I understand', she says, 'I think I lost you there. Could we go back to what happened with your brother?' This shows respect and keeps her with the client.
